sources.cite: AWS. SageMaker AI Developer Guide: Pre-training bias metrics (SageMaker Clarify)
sources.note: Read 2026-11-11: lists Class Imbalance (CI), Difference in Proportions of Labels (DPL), KL, JS, LP, TVD, KS and CDD. CI 'Measures the imbalance in the number of members between different facet values', normalized range [-1,+1]; DPL 'Measures the imbalance of positive outcomes between different facet values'.

sources.cite: AWS. SageMaker AI Developer Guide: Class Imbalance (CI)
sources.note: Read 2026-11-11: CI = (na - nd)/(na + nd); 'CI values near either of the extremes values of -1 or 1 are very imbalanced and are at a substantial risk of making biased predictions'; with significant imbalance 'you might want to rebalance the sample before proceeding to train models on it'. The page gives no numeric cutoff.

sources.cite: AWS. SageMaker AI Developer Guide: Difference in Proportions of Labels (DPL)
sources.note: Read 2026-11-11: DPL = qa - qd, the difference in the proportion of positive observed labels between facets; near 0 is 'demographic parity'.

sources.cite: AWS. SageMaker AI Developer Guide: Post-training data and model bias metrics
sources.note: Read 2026-11-11: eleven post-training metrics; DPPL 'Measures the difference in the proportion of positive predictions between the favored facet a and the disfavored facet d'; 'human judgment is required to understand and choose which metrics are relevant' and customers 'should consult with appropriate stakeholders'.

sources.cite: Kapoor S, Narayanan A. Leakage and the Reproducibility Crisis in ML-based Science. arXiv:2207.07048, 2022
sources.note: Read 2026-11-11: taxonomy item L1.2 'Pre-processing on training and test set': 'using oversampling before splitting the data into training and test sets leads to an imperfect separation'; L1.4 'Duplicates in datasets': 'the same data could exist in the training as well as test set.'

brief.situation: Monday 09:00. You are the ML engineer on a credit union's small-loan approval model, trained on SageMaker AI in us-east-2 (Ohio). In a pilot the model approves applicants under 25 far less often than older applicants with similar finances, though its test AUC was 0.91. The model risk team wants a retrained candidate this week.
handover: Training data: branch applications from 2019 to 2026 merged with the new online channel (2025-2026), about 10,000 rows. Age group is recorded for fairness testing.
The data scientist who built it has left. Notes say the split was 'the usual 80/20'.
Policy: a lending model ships only after a model risk review of its bias report, with the approval gap between age groups (DPPL) at 0.10 or less.
howItWorks: Learner-paced: nothing moves until you act. Investigate the data, change how it is prepared, choose how to release, then run the week.
The meters show the approval gap the candidate would produce and its reported test AUC.
Before you run the week you are asked where the bias came from and how you fixed it. The debrief scores what you did.

plan.question: Before you run the week: where did the bias come from, what did you change in the data, and how will you show the new model is fair enough to release?

parts.label: Sources of bias
parts.criteria: Names the class imbalance (CI 0.84), the unshuffled date split that left even fewer under-25 rows in training, and the policy-era labels; uses Clarify metrics as evidence.
parts.modelAnswer: Under-25 applicants are 8% of the rows (CI 0.84) and approved at half the rate in the labels (DPL 0.31). The date-ordered, unshuffled split put most online, younger applicants in test, leaving 4% in training. The 2019-2021 labels carry a retired policy against short credit histories.

parts.label: Mitigation and proof
parts.criteria: Shuffles and stratifies the split; oversamples or augments in the training split only, after splitting, to avoid leakage; does not rely on dropping age, since proxies remain; releases only through review with a post-training bias report (DPPL).
parts.modelAnswer: Shuffle and split stratified by age group and label, then oversample under-25 rows only in the training split so no copy reaches the test set. Dropping age would leave credit-history length as a proxy. Send a post-training bias report to model risk review and release only if DPPL is within 0.10.

expertPath.text: Clarify pre-training report: CI 0.84, DPL 0.31. The notebook: an unshuffled date split. The labels: a retired policy in 2019-2021.
Shuffle and stratify the split; oversample under-25 rows in the training split only; exclude the policy-era labels.
Post-training bias report to model risk review. The trade-off: AUC reads 0.86 instead of 0.91, because it is now measured honestly, and the release waits a day for review.

unreviewed.headline: Shipped without the bias review
unreviewed.body: A lending model's fairness is a release gate, not a follow-up. Whatever the data work, shipping before the review put an unproven model in front of applicants.

fixed.headline: Bias found, fixed and proven
fixed.body: You measured before changing, fixed the split, rebalanced without leaking and let the review prove the result. That is the expert path.

partly.headline: Better, by a rougher route
partly.body: Check whether you measured first, whether the split was shuffled and stratified, whether oversampling happened after the split, and whether the candidate went through review.

time_up.headline: No decision
time_up.body: The pilot keeps the biased model.

scoring.modelReasoning: Bias here has three sources: too few under-25 rows (CI 0.84), labels that reflect a retired policy (DPL 0.31), and a split that sorted by date without shuffling, which left even fewer young applicants in training. Fix the split first (shuffle, stratify by facet and label), then rebalance only the training split: oversampling before the split copies rows into the test set and inflates its scores, which is leakage. Dropping the sensitive column does not remove bias when other features stand in for it. Finally measure the trained model with post-training metrics such as DPPL and let people decide whether it is fair enough to release.
